data.title: Veľký vrch at Divinka – a central hillfort of three eras
data.excerpt: The hillfort on Veľký vrch above Divinka is one of the largest fortifications in Slovakia: its ramparts enclose more than 12 ha on a hill at the spot height of 530.1 m, on the boundary between the Žilina and Bytča basins. They were built in three chronological horizons – in the Final Bronze Age, in the Late La Tène period and in the 9th century. Dr A. Petrovský-Šichman first examined the site in 1947; excavations concentrated on the acropolis followed in 1972–1973.
data.metaTitle: Veľký vrch at Divinka – a mighty central hillfort
data.metaDescription: A large central hillfort above Divinka: mighty ramparts enclosing over 12 ha, built in three horizons from the Final Bronze Age to the 9th century.

keyFacts.label: Number of chronological horizons of the fortification
keyFacts.value: 3 (the Final Bronze Age, the Late La Tène–Early Roman period, the 9th century)

keyFacts.label: Number of post holes from dwellings discovered

timeline.title: The earliest occupation of the cadastral area
timeline.description: Finds from the Palaeolithic (a quartz bladelet flake on the Všivák crag) and above all from the Neolithic and the Eneolithic (pottery, sherds of the Baden culture, a stone axe-hammer from the 3rd millennium) document the intensive use of the cadastral area of Divinka by the first farmers.

timeline.title: Construction of the original rampart
timeline.description: According to radiocarbon analysis, the original rampart was built in the 10th century BC, probably during the Final Bronze Age (phase HB1), on the site of an earlier unfortified hilltop settlement of the Lusatian culture.

timeline.title: Construction of the oppidum of the Púchov culture
timeline.description: The people of the Púchov culture built a mighty fortress (a stone rampart about 2 m wide) on the older fortification from the Final Bronze Age; the hillfort became a centre of production, trade and the striking of silver coins of the Divinka type.

timeline.title: Destruction of the hillfort by the Germanic peoples
timeline.description: The hillfort was destroyed during a devastating invasion of the Germanic peoples, which also destroyed the other hillforts in northern Slovakia and caused a considerable destruction of the population.

timeline.title: The demise of the Púchov culture
timeline.description: By order of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius the Cotini were deported at the end of the Marcomannic Wars to the Roman province of Pannonia, whereby at the end of the 2nd century AD the Púchov culture ceased to exist as part of the occupation of this territory.

timeline.title: The growth of Slavic occupation in the basins
timeline.description: An unprecedented development of occupation came in the 8th–9th centuries, when the whole of the Žilina and Bytča basins was already occupied, as documented by dozens of settlements and extensive barrow cemeteries in the surroundings.

timeline.title: Slavic refortification of the hillfort
timeline.description: The Slavic population made use of the clearly visible old ramparts to fortify the site again, emphasised by a wooden palisade, and built log dwellings on stone footings on the acropolis.

timeline.title: The demise of the Slavic occupation of the hillfort
timeline.description: Finds of iron combat knives and half an iron spur on the crest of the rampart document hard fighting between the local defenders and new attackers of their own, Slavic stock, at the time of the formation of the Principality of Nitra or of Great Moravia.

timeline.title: Northern Slovakia joined to Great Moravia
timeline.description: In the second half of the 9th century northern Slovakia became part of Great Moravia, although the process did not proceed smoothly and the local tribes resisted it.

timeline.title: The rise of the medieval small fort Hradisko
timeline.description: On the neighbouring hill of Hradisko (cadastral area of Divina) a small medieval fort, the seat of a local feudal lord, arose at the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries, as a brief episode continuing the former glory of the hillfort.

timeline.title: The demise of the small fort Hradisko
timeline.description: The small fort was destroyed perhaps as early as the 13th century; trial trenches made in 1982 directly into the crest of the rampart revealed, besides pottery, strongly burnt layers, evidence of the destruction of the small fort.

timeline.title: The first modern excavation
timeline.description: Dr A. Petrovský-Šichman was the first to examine the hillfort in modern times and made the first sketch of the ramparts, which he sent to Prof. Vojtech Budinský-Krička.

timeline.title: Rescue excavation at Ohrádza
timeline.description: During the construction of the Hričov reservoir Petrovský-Šichman carried out a rescue archaeological excavation at the locality known as Ohrádza, where he obtained over 3,000 pottery sherds and settlement features with hearths.

timeline.title: Systematic excavation of the acropolis
timeline.description: The Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra and the Považie Museum in Žilina carried out an excavation in the summer months of 1972 and 1973 concentrated on the acropolis, which revealed two construction phases of the rampart and many key finds.

children.text: The hillfort was first examined in modern times by Dr Petrovský-Šichman in 1947. Separate excavations at the hillfort on Veľký vrch at Divinka took place in 1972–1973. As the archaeologist of the Považie Museum in Žilina, Dr Jozef Moravčík, noted in his article Opevnenia severozápadného Slovenska (Fortifications of north-western Slovakia). (2002 VZP XXI: 7–36), "the finds and the results of the excavations have not so far been systematically processed or comprehensively published. In the case of Divinka this is a large central hillfort, placed at the spot height of 530.1 and fortified with mighty ramparts that were built in three chronological horizons. The total fortified area exceeds 12 ha and the system of ramparts encircles the upper part of the spot height, situated on the boundary between the Žilina and Bytča basins (Moravčík 1980a, 19, 30). The use of the site is dated to three chronological horizons: 1. the Late to Final Bronze Age, 2. the Late
La Tène
to the Early Roman period, 3. and then the 9th century."

Mr Moravčík has provided our website with an extremely interesting article on the history of the hillfort, which you will not find anywhere else. I would like to take this opportunity to thank him for his helpful approach and his cooperation.

blocks.caption: The structure of the hillfort (by G. Fusek 2014)
blocks.alt: The structure of the hillfort (by G. Fusek 2014)

children.text: "Divinka is one of those villages whose occupation is documented deep into prehistory. The very first finds from the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic already suggested that we have here an exceptionally rich area of the earliest occupation. A quartz bladelet flake found on the Všivák crag indicates occupation of this area as early as the Old Stone Age, but far more intensive are the finds from the New Stone Age ( the Neolithic ) and from the Late Stone Age ( the Eneolithic ). In the field below the Všivák crag Ľ. Hroš found pottery of the Neolithic period, and A. Petrovský-Šichman found sherds of the Baden culture of the Eneolithic period directly on Veľký vrch. A stone axe-hammer from the 3rd millennium was also found in nearby Divina. It is therefore more than likely that already in the 4th–3rd millennium BC the cadastral area of Divinka was intensively used by the first farmers as well, who at that time began to cultivate the landscape here and to build their first permanent settlements.

children.text: The most important site in the cadastral area of the village is, however, the hillfort on Veľký vrch, otherwise also called Bučník ( probably after the beech trees that still grow here today, mainly on the northern slope of the hill ). The hillfort lies on the boundary between the Žilina and Bytča basins, directly above the Hričov reservoir, and is one of the most important fortifications of northern Slovakia, which became significant economic and cultural centres in at least three chronological horizons: in the Final Bronze Age, in the Late La Tène period and in the 9th century. Nor do the fortifications on Veľký vrch rank among the smallest; quite the contrary, even today mighty ramparts can be seen here, encircling not only the upper plateau of the hill but also a wide area on its northern side, so that the total fortified area reaches 12 ha. Dr A. Petrovský-Šichman called the fortification at Divinka the largest prehistoric stronghold in northern Slovakia and regarded it as the central stronghold of the north Slovak tribe in the 9th century.

blocks.caption: The presumed appearance of the hillfort in the La Tène period (the Púchov culture); 3D model by Naj
blocks.alt: The presumed appearance of the hillfort in the La Tène period (the Púchov culture); 3D model by Naj

children.text: Alexander Lombardíni wrote about the hillfort at Divinka as early as 1885 in Slovenské pohľady. He described not only the mighty ramparts: on the southern side 1 fathom high and 790 paces long, but also the cistern on the northern side of the fortification, in which rainwater was collected. He also mentions the oldest inhabitant of Divinka, the 85-year-old Ján Kišoň, who recounted that about 72 years earlier even the rubble of walls could still be seen at the highest point of the hillfort. About 60 years earlier Ján Kišoň had found an iron spear at a depth of two feet (strevíce) below the entrenchments (šiance) of Veľký vrch in the Bukovina wood, and Eva Stražanová is said to have found a gold hook here at that time. How much of what is in A. Lombardíni's article is true we can no longer say with certainty today, but the fact remains that the hillfort on Veľký vrch is among the most important sites in the whole territory of Slovakia and its significance can be compared with such fortifications as Devín, Nitra, Bratislava, Liptovská Mara, Spišský hrad and others. The hillfort played an important role in the shaping of occupation in at least three chronological horizons of the earliest periods, while its surroundings too were intensively occupied at least in the Late and Final Bronze Age, in the period around the turn of the era and then in the 8th–9th centuries.

children.text: The hillfort on Veľký vrch at Divinka was studied most intensively by Dr A. Petrovský-Šichman, who as early as 1947 also made the first sketch of the ramparts, which he sent to his teacher at the Department of Archaeology in Bratislava, Prof. Vojtech Budinský-Krička, DrSc. In 1955–1959 he began to devote himself more intensively to the surrounding terrain as well, and during the construction of the Hričov reservoir he carried out a rescue archaeological excavation at the locality known as Ohrádza, where an extensive settlement from several periods of prehistory and of the early historical period was situated.   During observations in 1955 he noticed that archaeological finds were absent from the neighbouring localities of Štvrtce and Putnisko, and therefore during the excavation of 1959 he concentrated solely on the area of Ohrádza. Here he managed to identify settlement features with hearths, continuous layers of stones which may have been the floors of dwellings, but above all an enormous quantity of pottery fragments ( over 3,000 diagnostic sherds ), which dated the occupation here to at least 2–3 chronological horizons. The most intensive occupation was the settlement of the people of the Lusatian culture from the Early Iron Age, then the settlement of the Púchov culture from the Late La Tène to the Early Roman period, and sherds of Slavic vessels were also found sporadically. For the first time in northern Slovakia it was also possible to record finds of Dacian and Quadic pottery. This means that the influences of the Dacians and the Quadi from southern Slovakia reached as far as these parts, whether through a direct presence in the milieu of the Púchov culture or rather through exchange trade with the local producers. Only a few sherds come from vessels imported from the Roman provinces, which at the same time makes it possible to date the occupation here as late as the Roman period, that is to the time when the hillfort itself had already been destroyed by the invasion of the Germanic peoples that took place in the first decades AD. A few small finds from the Early Roman period were also recorded in the foundations of Jozef Faltýn's extension in 1975. So life in the surroundings of the hillfort did not cease even when the fortifications on Veľký vrch had already been abandoned.

blocks.caption: A view of Veľký vrch at a time when it was not wooded (from the archive of Jozef Jaroš)
blocks.alt: A view of Veľký vrch at a time when it was not wooded (from the archive of Jozef Jaroš)

children.text: The most unique find from the surroundings of the settlement at Ohrádza is a gold earring, which was found in the 1960s during the prosaic work of digging potatoes in a field. It was found by the sister of Mr Kišoň, a long-serving and conscientious worker of the Považie Museum in Žilina. Together with a similar specimen from Orava–Veľký Bysterec, the earring is an outstanding testimony to the jewellery-making craft of the people of the Púchov culture. Both can currently be seen in the Klenoty Slovenska (Treasures of Slovakia) exhibition at Bratislava Castle. After this brief excursion into the history of the Divinka – Veľký vrch hillfort we can finally turn to clarifying the evidence that led to its exceptional position in the territory of northern Slovakia.   When in February 1971 the company Geologický prieskum Žilina began test trenching at the Veľký vrch site in order to obtain a suitable place for the extraction of material for the construction of the motorway, it was apparent that they had disturbed not only the original settlement layers but in several places also the earthen ramparts that encircled the central part of the hillfort, the acropolis. During an inspection of the site, a Late La Tène brooch made of so-called white metal ( an alloy of copper and tin with a higher tin content ) was found in the spoil thrown out of a trench laid on the southern slope of the acropolis. In both its design and its state of preservation ( it is completely intact ) the brooch had no parallel in the territory of Slovakia at that time. It belongs to the Almgren 66 type ( the classification of La Tène and Roman brooches by the Swedish scholar Olaf Almgren, which he published in Leipzig as early as 1923 ) and similar finds come from the Celtic oppida of Třísov and Stradonice in Bohemia. With its perfect form and excellent preservation it ranks among the unique examples of Late La Tène brooches, which were produced in the period around the middle of the 1st century BC. Further finds as well, especially pottery of the Lusatian and Púchov cultures, suggested that a trial archaeological excavation should be carried out here, one that could clarify the individual phases of the occupation of the hillfort and at the same time highlight its significance in the history of Slovakia, which until then could only be guessed at.

children.text: After intensive negotiations with the geologists in Žilina and at the hillfort itself, the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra and the Považie Museum in Žilina decided to carry out an excavation on Veľký vrch in the summer months of 1972, which was subsequently extended into the summer of 1973 as well. Since, according to the plans for the extraction of material, the central part of the hillfort was to be the most damaged, we concentrated the excavation directly on the acropolis. The very first trenches on the western plateau of the acropolis showed that the find situation here would be exceptionally complicated and that identifying the individual layers and chronological horizons would be very demanding, since the individual finds from different periods lay close beside one another ( for example, Great Moravian sherds were next to brooches ). In places the occupation layer reached only a few centimetres, because the rocky bedrock came right up to the surface.
Finds from the excavations of Dr Jozef Moravčík:

children.text: Finds of pottery made on the potter's wheel proved that this was not only a centre of production of this refined pottery, but that the surrounding settlements of the people of the Púchov culture were also supplied with these products. The favourable position of the hillfort above the old trade route which had run along the Váh since the earliest times predestined the fortification to become the central site for the Žilina and Bytča basins, where not only production and trade were concentrated, but also the strategic strength of the local people, who in time of attack could gather all their property here. After precisely surveying all the ramparts we estimated
the total fortified area at over 12 ha.
This makes the hillfort at Divinka
one of the largest fortifications in Slovakia.
We may regard it as an oppidum of the people of the Púchov culture, who built a mighty fortress here on an older fortification dating back to the Final Bronze Age.

blocks.caption: Iron objects – small knives, a small harpoon, on the left a plane, on the right the head of a large rivet
blocks.alt: Iron objects – small knives, a small harpoon, on the left a plane, on the right the head of a large rivet

children.text: In 1973 this assumption was fully confirmed when we cut through the southern rampart of the acropolis and found that beneath the fortification of the Púchov culture from the 1st century BC, represented by a stone rampart about 2 m wide, there lay an older and mightier fortification – a rampart 4 m wide — built of large sandstone boulders which were reinforced with vertically set posts and horizontally laid beams. On the surface of the rampart we managed to identify sherds of a Hallstatt bowl, which were also found on the inner side of the fortification, and after reconstructing them we obtained a very fine, hard-fired bowl decorated on its flat rim with small applied bosses. The surface of the bowl is also perfectly burnished and it can be dated to the turn of the 9th and 8th centuries BC.    Further finds from around the rampart and from the settlement layers likewise documented that this area was intensively used in the Final Bronze Age, when the hillfort was experiencing the first period of its flowering. We were convinced of this once again after taking over new finds from Ľ. Hroš, which he had dug up during amateur excavations on the northern side of the fortification in Bukovina. The quantity of Lusatian pottery exceeded the finds obtained by excavation, and so already in the period of the Final Bronze Age we must assume an important centre of production here, and the people of the Lusatian culture concentrated their forces on building a central fortification which had its hinterland in the surrounding settlements identified not only at Ohrádza but also in Žilina, Závodie and Stražov, and likewise in the circle of cemeteries discovered at Žilina, Marček, Svederník and Kotešová, which thus complete the overall picture of the occupation of the surroundings of the hillfort in the Final Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age.

children.text: Photographs from Dr Moravčík's excavations:

The hillfort on Veľký vrch experienced far more intensive occupation, however, in the 1st century BC, when a whole complex of ramparts arose here again, encircling not only the central part of the hill but also the northern slopes as far as the Divinka stream. Finds of over 50 post holes from the dwellings of that time, which were built immediately beside the inner face of the rampart, speak of a dense built-up area that must have been repeated several times over the whole duration of the occupation, at least from the middle of the 1st century BC to the years AD 20–30, when the hillfort was destroyed once again. Remains of hearths ( burnt areas of stones ), smithing workshops ( layers of ash and pieces of iron smithing slag ), domestic pottery as well as perfect pottery made on the potter's wheel, many iron and bronze objects: brooches, mounts, small knives, a shield handle, a cowrie sea shell imported all the way from the Adriatic, a fragment of an amber bead and other finds document the intensive life on the hillfort right up to its tragic end.
The demise of this phase of the occupation took place during the devastating invasion of the Germanic peoples,

which destroyed not only all the hillforts in northern Slovakia, but its perpetrators also brought about to an unprecedented degree a considerable destruction of the population, so that the continuation of the development of the Púchov culture in the following two centuries took place in a much smaller territory and with lesser intensity. Whereas in the 1st century BC not only the whole territory of northern Slovakia was occupied, but also the Hron region, Upper Nitra, Spiš, north-eastern Moravia and even part of southern Poland around Kraków, in the Early Roman period this was already only the middle and upper Váh region, especially around Púchov, Žilina and Liptov.   The people of the
Púchov culture

built not only many fortifications in northern Slovakia, but based their economic development above all on the intensive cultivation of crops and the raising of domestic cattle, and on the extraction of local raw materials, especially iron ores, silver and gold. The evidence for this is not only the burnt remains of cereals found directly at Divinka: 4 kinds of wheat, oats, millet, barley, but also of pulses: peas, broad beans and lentils. We discovered them deposited directly in the area of the excavation in a pit dug into the rocky bedrock, around which there were three post holes from uprights, that is to say a kind of granary where supplies were stored for the needs of preserving life in time of attack. This way of storing food supplies is a unique solution for that time, when most supplies were stored in storage pits or in large clay storage vessels. The hillfort on Veľký vrch did not escape its fate either. A large bronze brooch of the Almgren 67 type, which belongs to the first decades AD, is proof that the invasion of the Germanic peoples came unexpectedly and destroyed the whole hillfort (burnt layers of stones were found right on the surface of trench I ), but it did not spare its wide surroundings either. During the excavation almost complete vessels were also found deposited close to the rampart, which people had hidden here for more peaceful times, but these never returned. Even whole layers of river pebbles, which we found by the southern rampart of the acropolis and which the defenders evidently used for throwing at the attacking enemy, were of no help in the defence of the fortification.   The hillfort ceased to fulfil its important economic, cultural and military function as the centre of the Žilina and Bytča basins. It waited for its new inhabitants, who a thousand years later became our Slavic ancestors. The significance of the La Tène occupation on Veľký vrch was also supported by
the find of a silver coin of the Divinka type
( the name is derived from the place of the find ), which at that time was the only representative of this kind of coin, and
they were probably struck directly at Divinka

. Today we already have several of these finds: one specimen comes from the hillfort at Považský hrad, and 10–12 pieces were found at the smaller fortification of Hradište at Nozdrovice. Silver coins struck in the milieu of the Púchov culture are among the most precious things that can be found at the sites of northern Slovakia. That is why they are now also the reason for the greatest looting of the hillforts and small forts of the Púchov culture and for their sale abroad. Among the most precious finds is the discovery of a silver coin of the Nitra type at the small fort of Predná hôrka at Jasenica, which aroused well-deserved admiration among specialists, because it is the only coin of the 15 pieces known so far that has a precise find spot.   All these coins were struck at the central hillforts of the individual tribes of the Púchov culture, which we currently associate with the Celtic tribe of the Cotini. By order of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, however, at the end of the Marcomannic Wars they were deported to the Roman province of Pannonia because they had refused help to the Roman legions in their hard battles against the Germanic Marcomanni and Quadi and the Sarmatian Iazyges during the military operations in the territory of present-day Slovakia in the years 166–180. Thus at the end of the 2nd century AD the Púchov culture also came to an end, because its most important component had been deported outside its mother territory. This culture formed an important element of the occupation of Slovakia in the period from the 3rd century BC to the end of the 2nd century AD. At that time northern Slovakia also came to the attention of the Roman historians Tacitus and Ptolemy, who mention the Celtic Cotini as capable producers of iron and of iron objects ( especially weapons ), with which they paid tribute ( dues ) to the Germanic Quadi. The Púchov culture became an inseparable part of the development of the occupation of Slovakia and inscribed itself permanently in the history of the territory of present-day Slovakia and in the cultural development of the country. Even today, after the two millennia that have passed since the period of its maximum development, we must admire the quality of its products, the unique jewellery and the perfect pottery, which represents the advanced potters' workshops of northern Slovakia and can boldly be compared with similar finds from southern Slovakia, where the Celts had been settled ever since the turn of the 5th and 4th centuries BC.   The last stage of the fortification of the hillfort at Divinka on Veľký vrch is the 9th century.
The Slavic occupation

of northern Slovakia has its beginnings as early as the turn of the 5th and 6th centuries. From this period we have so far only a single settlement feature, which was found in Žilina at Frambor, but in the future further sites with early Slavic pottery may come to light. An unprecedented development of occupation came only in the 8th–9th centuries, when the whole of the Žilina and Bytča basins was already occupied. Dozens of settlements and extensive barrow cemeteries ( Krasňany – 51 graves, Bánová – 33 graves, Bitarová – over 30 graves ) prove that life in this territory continued with the same intensity as in earlier ages.
Divinka once again became the centre of Slavic occupation in this territory

, with its great hillfort. The mighty ramparts of earlier ages, which must have been clearly visible even in the 9th century, were put to use by the Slavic population to fortify the site again and to emphasise them with a wooden palisade as well, which raised the level of the defence. On the hillfort the Slavic population was already building log dwellings on stone footings, which it was possible to identify at two places on the acropolis of the hillfort during the excavation in 1973.

children.text: Slavic pottery did not attain such technical perfection as La Tène pottery, but even so, in the 9th century they already knew at least the hand-turned potter's wheel, on which they made simple pots by wheel-finishing, often richly decorated with horizontal bands of grooves and of multiple wavy lines. The Slavic people did not hold out long at the hillfort at Divinka. The fate of their predecessors befell them too. Finds of iron combat knives and half an iron spur found directly on the crest of the rampart speak plainly of the fact that here again there took place
hard fighting between the local defenders
and new attackers, this time, however, of their own stock – Slavic,
at the time of the formation of the Principality of Nitra
, or of Great Moravia. The military retinues of Pribina, Mojmír, Rastislav and Svatopluk had the task of
annexing the peripheral areas to the central parts of the territories as well.

This often happened by military means and by direct intervention in the environment of the local population. In the second half of the 9th century northern Slovakia too was already part of Great Moravia, even though this process certainly did not proceed smoothly and the local tribes certainly resisted it. One of the pieces of evidence for the presence of military retinues in northern Slovakia sent here from the central parts of Great Moravia are also the two warriors' graves examined in barrow no. 2 at Bánová, where men of tall stature were buried, armed with axes, knives, arrowheads and fire-steels. At the same time it is so far the only grave with such an arrangement in the whole territory of northern Slovakia, whereas in the other barrows cremation and inhumation graves were located only at the original ground level.

children.text: The spread of the new religion – Christianity – among the local people is also indicated by the find of the bezel of a bronze finger ring with a fourfold punched cross. It may have belonged to a local ruler, or perhaps to a priest who ventured into this inhospitable region and came to spread the new faith. How it really was we can only surmise, but the find of the object itself already suggests that the process of Christianisation was taking place in northern Slovakia too, just as in the other parts of Great Moravia. It was first accepted by the leading stratum of society and then by the rest of the people.   The hillfort at Divinka on Veľký vrch thus went through three phases of intensive development but also three demises of its occupation. The last of these permanently interrupted life behind the rampart fortifications of this important centre of northern Slovakia. All fell dead here and only shepherds with their cattle occasionally strayed in ( finds of milk jugs from the 18th–19th centuries ) and perhaps remembered the bygone glory of the stronghold that once stood here and protected the whole territory of the Žilina and Bytča basins. Today we can only imagine what life was like at this important hillfort, but how it really was is only a part of what we managed to uncover during the archaeological excavations.   The years of development, the falls and rebirths of the fortress took place in several stages, which recurred with regular intensity always when the local people managed to achieve a marked development of their creative powers. Perhaps this at the same time became the cause of the three repeated demises of the occupation of the hillfort, which was certainly known far and wide as an important strategic site and at the same time as an economically important centre of the people of the Lusatian culture, of the Púchov culture and of our Slavic ancestors.    A brief episode continuing the former glory of the hillfort on Veľký vrch at Divinka still took place on
the neighbouring hill of Hradisko
, which already lies in the cadastral area of Divina, where at the turn of the
12th and 13th centuries

a small medieval fort arose, the seat of a local feudal lord. This too was destroyed perhaps as early as the 13th century, since during trial trenches made here in 1982 directly into the crest of the rampart, in addition to pottery, strongly burnt layers were also found, which are evidence of the destruction of the small fort. With a little imagination we could assume that
the local owner of the feudal estate may have been a direct heir to the bygone glory of his Slavic predecessors

, who so successfully built the enormous fortification on Veľký vrch at Divinka.   In conclusion we should at least mention the further finds of intensive occupation of the cadastral area of the village, which we know from the period from the Neolithic to the early Middle Ages. At the locality known as Tomášovec traces of occupation of the Púchov culture were identified. At the locality known as Háj there may also have been a fortification; there are artificially modified terraces here. Vrtielky – a settlement of the Púchov and possibly also of the Lusatian culture. Všivák – a crag with occupation from the La Tène and the Roman periods. Za Malým Všivákom – occupation from the Early Iron Age. Za potokom v agáte – a Púchov settlement. V Priekope Studeného potoka – a settlement of the Púchov culture. Nivy – a settlement of the Púchov culture. Pod Loviškami – a settlement of the Púchov culture. Pri Všiváku – a settlement of the Púchov culture. Za Malým Všivákom – a settlement of the Púchov culture and also from the Early Iron Age. Pri kaplnke – a settlement from the Late Stone Age and of the Púchov culture.   From the mere listing of the individual find spots it is clear that the most intensive occupation in the cadastral area of Divinka belongs to the Púchov culture of the Late La Tène period, when the hillfort on Veľký vrch was also experiencing the time of its greatest flowering. Apart from the settlement of the Lusatian culture at Ohrádza, other localities of this period are occupied in the Early Iron Age as well, because the people of the Lusatian culture settled permanently in the valleys of northern Slovakia and survived here until the Late Iron Age. At that time, with the contribution of Celtic incomers, they also created the Púchov culture as a material expression of the development of the occupation of this territory.   To list all the finds together with their detailed description would require publishing a separate book, but for the purposes for which this contribution is made that is not even necessary. What matters is the realisation that Divinka already belonged among the most important sites of Slovakia 2–3 millennia ago, and its status can no longer be overturned even by the newest finds from other regions of our homeland. At least three times in the course of the ages it inscribed itself in the awareness of the wide surroundings and its significance long ago exceeded the boundaries of the region of north-western Slovakia."

children.text: The assessment of the dating of the fortification by the authors G. Fusek and M. Holeščák from 2019 gives the following dating of the hillfort's fortification:

"The excavation of the fortification of the summit area of the hillfort at Divinka yielded important evidence for dating its construction. According to the results of radiocarbon analysis, the original rampart was built here in the 10th century BC, probably during the Final Bronze Age (phase HB1). Its bank contained pottery of the Late to the beginning of the Final Bronze Age, testifying that before the fortification was built there was an unfortified hilltop settlement of the Lusatian culture on Veľký vrch. After the surface of the collapsed rampart bank had been levelled almost two millennia later, in the Great Moravian period, it served as the base for the construction of a new rampart. In the La Tène phase of the occupation of the site, a small area of today's acropolis was separated off from the summit part of the hillfort by a rampart, thereby creating a small fort whose enclosed area was intensively occupied. At that time the other parts of the hillfort were used to a reduced extent. The section through the fortification in the settlement below the hillfort (suburbium) likewise documented two stages of its construction. The later one is dated by radiocarbon analysis to the Great Moravian period. The field excavation yielded no evidence for the chronological attribution of the original rampart. Proceeding from the overall situation at the site and from the described results of the excavation of the fortification in its higher-lying parts, we assume that it was built at the same time as the circuit fortification of the summit part of the hillfort. We are led to this consideration by the logical reasoning that if in the La Tène period there was a reason to build a small fort on the summit of Veľký vrch and the ramparts on the perimeter of the hill ridge were not renewed, then they evidently did not renew the extensive abandoned fortification on the slopes of the hill below it either. In the Great Moravian period they made use of the abandoned ramparts of the entire mighty fortification system whose origin goes back to the Final Bronze Age."
